cards.title: Your AI Code is Watching You: The Looming Crisis of Invisible Injections and Hidden Data
cards.thesis: People are getting seriously fed up with tech companies, especially AI tools and big platforms like Cloudflare, quietly collecting their data or injecting stuff into their projects without asking. There's a growing demand for transparency and control over what happens with your digital creations and personal information, creating a huge trust deficit.

evidence.text: Cloudflare silently injected a JS analytics snippet into my HTML-only site when I switched nameservers. I had to go to the Analytics dashboard, add the site, and then disable the snippet. I find this approach entirely invasive, you should opt-in to features like that not...

I reverse engineered the latest Kimi Work desktop app and found something concerning: when you send a feedback report, it attaches the 5 latest sessions to the report with no notice or heads up or anything. These sessions could have ANYTHING in them, and you have no idea you're sending it all to Kimi.

A good proportion of us and our colleagues are now churning out agent-assisted code at an incredible rate... I'm personally finding that the real quality gate for our projects is now how thoroughly the generated code was human reviewed to ensure that it is not just correct, but architecturally sensible.
I created a web browser using Claude, Gemini and Chatgpt Codex, everybody hates it, insults me personally and calls it AI slop.

Since the DDoS attack of 2024, Internet Archive has been hit or miss on uploading. This uncertainty causes me to break focus on working with music and watch the upload to make sure there isn't a 503 error happening each file.

cards.opportunity: People are freaking out because AI tools and big platforms are quietly messing with their code or sending private data without asking. Think about a simple browser extension or a local proxy (a mini program that sits between your computer and the internet, letting you see and control data) that acts like a bouncer, showing you *exactly* what an AI agent or a service like Cloudflare is trying to add to your website or send from your coding sessions *before* it happens. You could build a basic version that flags suspicious code injections or data transfers from common AI coding tools or web platforms, giving builders the control they're clearly desperate for.

cards.title: Ship Smart Sidekicks: AI-Powered Companions for Popular Apps
cards.thesis: Powerful AI models are getting tiny enough to run on your local machine (meaning, directly on your computer, not needing a cloud server), which is sparking a wave of builders creating small, focused 'companion tools' and extensions. These tools enhance popular existing software by automating specific, annoying tasks, often by processing or generating information for those apps, making workflows smoother for users.

evidence.text: Someone successfully 'shrank DeepSeek V4 Flash to 57GB and it wrote a compiler on my Mac,' showing powerful AI can run locally.
A 'Windows companion panel and docs for ExpressVPN setup' garnered 200 engagements, highlighting a demand for tools that streamline popular software workflows.

Another highly engaged project (172 engagements) is a 'Portable DS4Windows companion toolkit' with setup guides and helpers for game controllers, showing a clear need for workflow-specific enhancements.
A free open-source 'extractor for AI coding assistant chat histories' supports tools like Claude Code and Cursor, indicating a need to process and structure AI outputs from specific applications.
A 'Claude Code skill' that turns confirmed vulnerabilities into 'submission-ready DOCX reports' demonstrates how AI can be used to automate specific, structured output generation from other tools.

cards.opportunity: Everyone's shipping little companion tools for popular software, from ExpressVPN to Filmora, to fix annoying workflows or add missing features. Now that powerful AI models like DeepSeek V4 Flash can run locally on your machine, you can embed serious smarts into these tiny apps. Pick a popular tool with a super specific, repetitive task — like generating social media captions from a video editor's export, or summarizing a long chat log from a specific AI coding assistant — and build a lightweight, AI-powered sidekick that automates that one thing. Ship it as a free local app or a browser extension and watch the niche communities find you.

cards.title: AI's Reality Check: The Gold Rush for Reliable, 'Boring' Automation
cards.thesis: The initial hype around AI doing 'everything' is fading fast as builders and companies realize large language models (LLMs) frequently 'hallucinate' (make up information) and are too unreliable for critical tasks. This pullback is creating a massive demand for simple, lightweight tools that reliably automate tedious, data-heavy work where accuracy is non-negotiable, even if it's 'boring' automation.

evidence.text: Many companies have moved from 'use LLMs for anything and everything' to limiting budgets and scopes for AI usage, prompting questions about whether relying less on AI is economically viable for developers.
The persistent problem of AI 'hallucination' (when AI makes up facts or information) is still unsolved, leading to frustration and skepticism about its reliability.
Builders are actively seeking and valuing lightweight tools and command-line utilities that save countless hours by simply performing specific tasks reliably.

A tool like 'paperpull' shows real demand for 'read-only' utilities that log in to services (like Amazon, banks) to reliably download and archive personal data (receipts, statements) as PDFs, focusing on accurate collection rather than generation.

cards.opportunity: Everyone's realizing AI makes stuff up, but people still spend hours logging into different services to pull reports, reconcile numbers, or grab specific data points. Instead of trying to make AI *generate* content, build simple, 'read-only' automations that reliably *collect* and organize data from existing, trusted sources like specific APIs (which are just ways for apps to talk to each other) or web pages. There's a huge market right now for tools that guarantee accurate data collection from all those places where people currently copy-paste manually, like pulling specific metrics from dashboards or consolidating reports from different services.

cards.title: Real-time Multiplayer Experiences are Heating Up (Beyond Just Games)
cards.thesis: Builders are increasingly shipping real-time multiplayer apps, showing that the tools for creating shared, interactive experiences (where multiple people can do things together instantly) are becoming super accessible. This isn't just for traditional games; it signals a broader trend in collaborative online experiences.

evidence.text: A new 'Show HN' launched called 'Mic Drop,' which is a real-time multiplayer karaoke game, attracting 119 engagements on Hacker News.
Another 'Show HN' featured 'Side Out,' a multiplayer survival version of Pong, indicating continued interest in real-time interactive apps.

cards.opportunity: Everyone's playing around with real-time multiplayer games again, but the real untapped gold is applying that same tech to co-working, learning, or hyper-niche communities. Think 'Figma for X' where X is something currently stuck in static documents, or an interactive 'study room' where everyone can draw and chat in real-time. The underlying real-time communication tech is accessible enough now that you could prototype a unique collaborative tool for a specific niche community this weekend.

cards.title: Reddit Just Put Old.Reddit.com Behind a Login Wall — Your Move.
cards.thesis: Reddit just made a huge change, forcing everyone who prefers the classic 'old Reddit' interface to log in just to browse, even public pages. This creates immediate friction for a massive, vocal user base and an opening for simple tools that restore that beloved anonymous or simplified browsing experience.

evidence.text: The old.reddit.com site now requires a login, with users exclaiming, 'You maniacs! You blew it up!'
The page text explicitly states: 'Log in to use old Reddit. To keep Reddit safe, accounts are required to access old Reddit.'

cards.opportunity: Old Reddit users are furious they now have to log in just to browse, even for public content. There's an immediate opening for a browser extension or a simple web app that lets people see old Reddit content without constantly logging in, perhaps by securely storing credentials once or by caching what's still publicly accessible. Ship a minimal read-only viewer for popular subreddits this weekend, and you'll instantly grab a passionate user base.

cards.title: YC's Earliest Signals: What 'Founding' Roles Tell Builders
cards.thesis: Even YC companies in very early or future batches are immediately seeking core technical talent, signaling a strong emphasis on foundational product development and rigorous testing from the outset. This shows YC continues to back ventures requiring deep engineering expertise right from the start.

evidence.text: Gooseworks (YC W23) Is Hiring a Founding Builder / Engineer
Voltair (YC W26) Is Hiring a Test Flight Engineer

cards.opportunity: The fact that YC is funding companies like Voltair (W26, meaning they’re super early) and they’re already hiring 'Founding Builder' and 'Test Flight' engineers means they’re prioritizing getting core product out and rigorously tested from day one. This points to a gap in tools that help early-stage teams, especially those with complex products, set up automated, robust testing environments super fast. You could build a boilerplate or a Replit template that just *works* for setting up testing for specific complex use cases, like real-time data or hardware integrations.
